findings.headline: The historical MRP overpayment that has been subsidising revenue budgets will be fully consumed by end of 2026/27, creating a permanent revenue cost increase from 2027/28.
findings.detail: Wakefield has been using a longstanding MRP overpayment (from a 2016 policy change) to offset annual MRP charges. This buffer reduces from £12.5m at start of 2025/26 to £5.3m at year-end and 'will be fully utilised by the end of the 2026/27 financial year'. After that, all MRP charges will hit the revenue budget in full, requiring additional budget provision.
findings.matters: This represents a quantified and material increase in future revenue costs (approximately £7m+ annually based on current MRP levels) that will reduce financial flexibility unless revenue rises or other costs reduce to offset it.
findings.figures: MRP overpayment balance: £12.5m (start 2025/26), £5.3m (end 2025/26), zero (end 2026/27); MRP charged to revenue: £9.8m in 2025/26
findings.quote: The balance of the overpayment will be fully utilised by the end of the 2026/27 financial year. Thereafter, all MRP will be charged to the revenue budget and the impact has been reflected in the Council's Medium Term Financial Strategy.

findings.headline: Capital programme underspent significantly for the second consecutive year, with £54.9m less spent than budgeted.
findings.detail: Actual capital spend was £80.4m against budget of £135.3m (40% underspend). The paper notes 'significant slippage at the end of both 2024/25 and 2025/26'. While this reduced borrowing needs and saved £4.2m in interest costs, sustained underspend raises questions about execution capability.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether the council can deliver its investment plans. Two consecutive years of major slippage suggests potential execution or planning challenges that could affect service delivery and future financing needs.
findings.figures: £80.4m actual vs £135.3m budget; £4.2m borrowing cost saving
findings.quote: The capital programme had significant slippage at the end of both 2024/25 and 2025/26, reducing the need for the council to borrow externally, saving the council £4.2m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Flexible use of capital receipts strategy
findings.headline: Future-year transformation savings (2026/27–2029/30) are not yet quantified despite £5m+ in committed costs
findings.detail: The council achieved claimed revenue savings of £22.6m against transformation costs of £6.1m in 2024/25. However, the strategy table shows that transformation and severance costs for 2026/27–2029/30 (estimated at £4.75m) have all savings entries marked 'tbc' rather than specified amounts.
findings.matters: Committing capital expenditure without identified or quantified benefits creates execution risk; failure to deliver the expected transformation savings would force unexpected revenue reductions
findings.figures: 2024/25 actual costs £6,142k against savings £22,578k; 2026/27–2029/30 planned costs £4,751k with savings shown as 'tbc'
findings.quote: The Council will incur other project costs on its transformation journey and will look to utilise this directive to meet those costs, ensuring the maximum saving to the revenue budget is achieved

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Flexible use of capital receipts strategy
findings.headline: Wakefield has committed £11.9m of capital receipts for severance and transformation through 2029/30, following £10.5m cumulative spending from 2016–24 and £5.7m–£6.2m annually in recent years
findings.detail: The council is using the capital receipts flexibility to fund staff severance (primary cost) and transformation projects. Severance spending has been substantial: £10.5m cumulatively 2016–24, £5.7m in 2024/25, and £6.2m estimated for 2025/26. The forward strategy commits £11.9m across 2025/26–2029/30.
findings.matters: Sustained severance spending signals ongoing organizational restructuring; the council is using asset sales proceeds to fund personnel costs, which suggests revenue budgets are insufficient to absorb these costs
findings.quote: Capital receipts funding of £11.9m have been set aside for severance and other transformation costs across years 2025/26 to 2029/30

findings.headline: £28m High Needs Provision Capital Allowance concentrated in 2026/27–2027/28, rising to £9.5m peak
findings.detail: SEND capital provision (High Needs Provision Capital Allowance) is £27.9m over five years, peaking at £9.5m in 2027/28. This is non-discretionary spend; the council must fund it. Spend is concentrated in early years when grant funding is available, then drops sharply.
findings.matters: SEND provision is a statutory and non-discretionary spend; this large commitment must be funded regardless of other pressures. Lenders assess whether discretionary spending (regeneration) is crowding out essential services.
findings.quote: High Needs Provision Capital Allowance 3,203 6,878 9,505 4,200 4,200 27,986

findings.headline: Capital programme front-loaded with grants; spending cliff of 55% from 2027/28 to 2028/29
findings.detail: Total capital spending drops from £95.6m (2027/28) to £43.5m (2028/29), a 55% reduction. This cliff coincides with the collapse in government grants and reflects a programme built around time-limited external funding (Towns Fund, grant schemes) rather than sustainable priorities.
findings.matters: Lenders evaluate whether capital investment reflects enduring service need or temporary grant opportunity; a cliff in expenditure following grant expiry suggests the programme may not be aligned with the council's financial sustainability
findings.figures: 2027/28 total budget £95,631k; 2028/29 total budget £43,501k (reduction of £52,130k or 55%)

findings.headline: Identified funding falls short of stated budget by £1.3m in peak spending year 2026/27
findings.detail: The capital programme budget for 2026/27 is £130.3m but identified funding is only £128.9m, creating a shortfall of £1.3m in the year with highest planned spend. This funding gap in the programme's peak year suggests either unidentified sources or programme slippage.
findings.matters: A funding gap in the principal capital year indicates either understatement of borrowing need or risk that planned projects will not proceed; a finance director needs to explain the closed funding position
findings.figures: 2026/27 budget £130,334k vs funding £128,988k = shortfall of £1,346k

findings.headline: £115.9m prudential borrowing commitment (28% of total funding) to fund capital programme
findings.detail: The council plans to borrow £115.9m over five years using prudential borrowing powers, ranging from £16.8m (2028/29) to £26.7m (2026/27). This borrowing funds the capital programme and will require repayment from revenue budgets.
findings.matters: A lender assessing debt capacity needs to understand all committed borrowing obligations; £115.9m in new borrowing increases the council's overall debt burden and revenue financing requirements

findings.headline: Government grant funding cliffs from £62.7m to £9.9m between 2026/27 and 2028/29
findings.detail: Government grants comprise 39% of total capital funding at £162.4m, but drop 85% between 2026/27 and 2028/29 (from £62.665m to £9.870m). This 52.8m reduction forces the council to increase reliance on prudential borrowing to maintain programmes in later years.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand whether the council can sustain capital ambitions when external grant funding expires; grant dependency creates refinancing risk if regeneration objectives are not completed

findings.headline: Regeneration programme represents 53% of capital investment (£219.8m over five years) including new Muse strategic partnership
findings.detail: Regeneration, Environment & Economic Growth represents £219.8m (53%) of the £414.7m capital programme. In January 2025, Cabinet approved appointment of Muse as Strategic Regeneration Partner for Wakefield City to plan and deliver regeneration projects and leverage private sector investment. This represents a significant concentration of capital resources and commitment to a private sector partner.
findings.matters: Large-scale regeneration programmes carry execution risk, market sensitivity, and dependence on private sector delivery partners; concentration of 53% of capital spend in this area warrants monitoring of delivery and outcomes.
findings.figures: Regeneration capital programme: £219,767k (2025/26-2029/30); 53% of total capital spend
findings.quote: In January 2025, the Cabinet also approved the appointment of Muse as the Council's Strategic Regeneration Partner for Wakefield City. They will work with the Council to help plan, deliver, and develop new regeneration projects for our city as well as working to leverage in as much private sector investment as they can to support our strategic priorities.

findings.headline: Cessation of Bridge Homes and Business Rates Pool investments during 2025/26
findings.detail: The Council previously invested in Bridge Homes and a Business Rates Pool but has ended both during 2025/26. The document does not explain the reasons for cessation, but withdrawal from these investments suggests they were not delivering expected returns or had other issues requiring exit.
findings.matters: Investment failures or exits affect council finances and suggest reassessment of non-financial treasury investments; understanding why investments were ended is relevant to assessing investment decision-making quality.
findings.figures: Bridge Homes and Business Rates Pool investments ceased
findings.quote: Previous investments into Bridge Homes and Business rates pool have ceased during 2025/26.

findings.headline: Asset verification programme starting to identify property maintenance liabilities
findings.detail: During 2025 the council has commissioned a series of Asset Verification and Condition reports to inform long-term maintenance planning. Cabinet will receive update in Q2 of 2026/27 on outcomes. The Council holds £504.54m net book value of operational land and buildings assets and £86.2m in investment properties. This verification programme suggests systematic assessment of deferred maintenance and reinvestment requirements.
findings.matters: Asset condition reports typically reveal deferred maintenance liabilities that require future capital investment; this could indicate emerging pressures on capital budgets or funding requirements not yet quantified.
findings.figures: Operational assets: £504.54m net book value (31 March 2025); Investment properties: £86.2m net book value (31 March 2025)
findings.quote: During 2025 the council has commissioned a series of Asset Verification and Condition reports which will inform a long-term maintenance plan. The aim is to update Cabinet in quarter two of 2026/27 on the outcomes of the surveys.

findings.headline: Material change to MRP affordability framework: moving from fixed 6.5% threshold to flexible capital contingency allocation
findings.detail: The strategy updates the affordability approach by replacing the assumption that MRP does not exceed 6.5% of the Council's adjusted net revenue budget with approval of a capital contingency allocation within the main programme. Cabinet is permitted to allocate contingency to new or existing projects while remaining within affordability parameters. This represents a shift from a fixed rule to a more discretionary approach to managing debt repayment.
findings.matters: This change affects how tightly debt repayment is constrained; moving from an objective 6.5% rule to discretionary allocation creates greater flexibility but potentially less certainty about debt management discipline.
findings.figures: Previous threshold: MRP not to exceed 6.5% of adjusted net revenue budget
findings.quote: This strategy updates the approach to affordability through the approval of a capital contingency allocation within in the main programme. It is proposed that cabinet will be permitted to allocate this contingency to either new or existing projects whilst ensuring the programme remains within the affordability parameters identified at the time of finalising the budget each year. This approach replaces the assumption that MRP does not exceed 6.5% of the Council's adjusted net revenue budget.

findings.headline: £115.9m of prudential borrowing over five years representing 27.9% of the capital programme funding
findings.detail: The Council's capital programme is funded through prudential borrowing (27.9%), government grants (39.2%), other grants (17.2%), capital receipts (13.6%), and contributions (2.1%). Prudential borrowing creates revenue costs through interest charges and Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP). The borrowing increases the Council's capital financing requirement significantly.
findings.matters: A lender to the council needs to understand the scale of borrowing commitments and how they will be serviced through the revenue budget; this represents a material increase in debt obligations.
findings.quote: Prudential Borrowing - the Council can use this type of borrowing subject to the requirements of the prudential code for capital expenditure. It allows the Council to spread the cost of funding capital expenditure over the useful life of the asset. Prudential borrowing increases the Council's capital financing requirement and creates revenue costs through interest charges and the minimum revenue provision (MRP).

findings.paper_title: Capital Investment and Treasury Management Strategy 202627
findings.headline: Financial resources and organisational capacity identified as active strategic corporate risks
findings.detail: The Council's risk register identifies two strategic risks: (1) Financial resources risk due to cost pressures, limited funding, and insufficient resources to meet statutory duties with risk of budget overspend; (2) Organisational capacity risk from lack of workforce planning and multiple competing priorities. Both are flagged as material concerns.
findings.matters: Council-acknowledged risks around financial viability and delivery capacity directly affect the feasibility and financial resilience of a £414.7m capital programme and the council's ability to service the associated debt.
findings.figures: Two strategic risks: CORSTRR0057 (Financial resources), CORSTRR0109 (Organisational Priorities & Capacity)
findings.quote: Due to increasing cost pressures and demands for services, coupled with limited and volatile funding, there is a risk that there are insufficient financial resources available to support the delivery of Council strategic and statutory duties

findings.paper_title: Capital Investment and Treasury Management Strategy 202627
findings.headline: MRP and debt financing budget increased in revenue proposals following public consultation
findings.detail: The council's revenue budget proposals included increases to both Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) and debt financing budget, which were subject to public consultation closing 1 February 2026. These increases reflect growing debt service obligations as the capital programme is financed through borrowing.
findings.matters: Rising MRP and debt financing costs indicate the council's debt servicing burden is accelerating and will consume an increasing share of the revenue budget, constraining spending on other services and limiting financial resilience.
findings.figures: MRP and debt financing budget increases approved January 2026 (detailed in appendix 3)
findings.quote: The Council's initial revenue budget proposals, including an increase to the MRP and debt financing budget were approved by Cabinet on 13th January 2026

findings.paper_title: Capital Investment and Treasury Management Strategy 202627
findings.headline: Council committing £3.8m annual incremental revenue funding to finance the capital programme
findings.detail: The Medium Term Financial Strategy includes annual £3.8m of incremental revenue funding for each year through to 2029/30 to cover MRP (Minimum Revenue Provision) and capital financing costs. This removes reliance on capital reserves and represents new recurring revenue commitments to service the debt generated by the capital programme.
findings.matters: Dedicating £3.8m annually in revenue budget to capital financing represents a structural commitment that reduces flexibility for other services and signals the council is stretching its revenue budget to support ambitious capital ambitions.
findings.figures: £3.8m annual incremental revenue funding for each year of MTFS (£19m over 5 years)
findings.quote: annual £3.8m of incremental revenue funding provided for each year of the MTFS, removing the reliance on the capital reserve to support the cost of financing the programme

findings.paper_title: Capital Investment and Treasury Management Strategy 202627
findings.headline: Prudential borrowing of £115.9m finances 28% of the capital programme over five years
findings.detail: The capital programme relies on debt financing for £115.9m of the £414.7m total. Borrowing is highest in 2026/27 (£28.7m) and 2027/28 (£24.9m), declining to £15.1m in 2028/29 before rising again to £22.9m in 2029/30. This substantial and sustained borrowing will increase the council's debt servicing burden and constrain future financial flexibility.
findings.matters: Nearly three decades of the capital programme financed by debt means the council is committing to significant long-term debt service obligations that will reduce budget flexibility for other services and test the council's borrowing capacity.

findings.paper_title: Capital Investment and Treasury Management Strategy 202627
findings.headline: £2.05m redirected from Digital Strategy and Climate Change projects to highways resurfacing in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council has reallocated existing capital funding away from strategic digital transformation and climate change initiatives to fund highway resurfacing. Future years' highway funding will depend on finding savings elsewhere in the programme or drawing on the £3m capital contingency, indicating resource constraints and shifting priorities.
findings.matters: Cannibalizing digital and climate investments to fund routine maintenance suggests the council faces resource pressures and may struggle to deliver longer-term strategic objectives alongside essential upkeep.
findings.figures: £2.05m redirected in 2026/27; £3m contingency for future years
findings.quote: A total of £2.05m of funding for 2026/27 has been redirected and rephased. Funding for future years will be allocated from the £3m contingency, if savings from the existing capital programme cannot be found.

findings.paper_title: Capital Investment and Treasury Management Strategy 202627
findings.headline: Capital programme increased by £112m to reflect previously unbudgeted recurring maintenance and grant-eligible spending
findings.detail: The council's review identified that the capital programme did not adequately reflect recurring expenditure for Property & Facilities Long Term Maintenance, Disabled Facilities Grants, General School Condition Grants, and High Needs Provision Capital Allowance. These £112m of additions represent a 27% upward revision, indicating the baseline programme substantially underestimated recurring annual commitments.
findings.matters: The discovery of £112m in unbudgeted recurring costs signals forecasting weakness and reveals a maintenance and grant-eligible backlog that will now require additional borrowing or revenue support, directly affecting the council's debt trajectory and financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £112m injections identified; total capital programme revised to £414.7m (2025/26 to 2029/30)
findings.quote: The programme requires injections of £112m to cover issues including Property & Facilities Long Term Maintenance Plan, Disabled Facilities Grant, General School Condition Grant and High Needs Provision Capital Allowance.

findings.headline: The Council is borrowing an additional £3.8m for capital financing in 2026/27 to meet capital programme requirements.
findings.detail: The budget includes an additional £3.8m in revenue provision for new borrowing requirements to fund the Council's capital programme, and reflects the medium-term strategy to increase the minimum revenue provision (MRP) budget to sustainable levels.
findings.matters: Increasing capital debt service obligations reduce the flexibility to respond to demand pressures and represents a structural lock-in of future revenue costs.
findings.figures: £3.8m additional MRP/debt service provision for 2026/27
findings.quote: An additional provision of £3.8m has been included in the revenue budget to reflect new borrowing requirements to fund the council's capital programme and as part of the medium-term strategy to increase the minimum revenue provision budget to sustainable levels that don't require annual one-off funding from the capital reserve.

findings.headline: Inflation adds £14m to the Council's 2026/27 budget, with limited scope to absorb further price rises.
findings.detail: The Council estimates that inflation will add approximately £14m to costs, including £6.9m for pay awards and £9.7m in fee and charges increases, partially offset by a £6.4m reduction in pension contribution rates.
findings.matters: Large inflation impact reduces financial flexibility. If actual inflation exceeds the £14m provision or pay awards run higher, the council will face in-year pressure with limited reserves to call on.
findings.figures: £14m inflation provision; £6.9m pay award; £9.7m fees and charges; (£6.4m) pension rate reduction
findings.quote: The effect of inflation on the Council's 2026/27 revenue budget is substantial, adding an estimated £14m to costs (see section 3.5 for details).

findings.headline: Staffing restructuring costs have exceeded the original flexible use of capital receipts budget and required strategy revision.
findings.detail: The cost of voluntary redundancy and severance packages has exceeded what was identified in the original Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Strategy. The council has updated the strategy for 2025/26 and forecasted 2026/27 to accommodate higher-than-expected severance spending.
findings.matters: Restructuring costs running over their plan suggests either organisational change is larger than anticipated or severance terms are proving more costly, both indicators of organisational stress during a tight budget period.
findings.figures: No specific overrun amount disclosed in main text
findings.quote: The cost of severance packages will exceed the level identified in the original Flexible Use of Receipts Strategy and as such this strategy document (appendix 6) provides an update for 2025/26 as well as a forecast for 2026/27

findings.headline: Grant Thornton's 2024/25 audit specifically warned the Council against using general financial resilience reserves to balance the budget or manage in-year overspends.
findings.detail: The external auditor's value-for-money report (being presented to Audit Committee on 16 February 2026) reinforced that the Council should not use reserves as a balancing mechanism. This reflects concerns raised in January 2025 about the Council's reserve management practices.
findings.matters: External audit concern about reserve sustainability is a governance red flag and suggests the auditor views the Council's earlier reliance on reserves as a risk factor in financial resilience.
findings.figures: Not quantified; timing: audit presented 16 February 2026
findings.quote: It is important to note that the 2024/25 value for money audit report from Grant Thornton which is being presented to Audit Committee on 16th February 2026 reinforced the need for the Council to refrain from planned use of general financial resilience reserves to balance the budget (or as a way to manage in-year overspends).

findings.headline: Housing Benefits continue to be a structural funding pressure, with DWP subsidy not covering full costs, particularly for supported accommodation.
findings.detail: The Council reports ongoing pressure on Housing Benefits because the Department for Work and Pensions does not fully subsidise costs through its subsidy arrangements. The gap is particularly acute for supported accommodation. The council is reviewing options to mitigate the funding gap (detailed in Appendix 1).
findings.matters: This is a recurring, structural deficit between what the DWP reimburses and what the Council must pay, with no clear solution yet and requiring ongoing mitigations or absorbing the cost within the budget.
findings.figures: No specific figure provided in main text
findings.quote: Housing Benefits continue to be a pressure for the Council with DWP not fully covering costs through its subsidy arrangements, with the differential between costs and subsidy on supported accommodation being a significant issue. The council is reviewing options to mitigate the funding gap, further details in Appendix 1.

findings.headline: The Council must deliver £11.5m of savings to balance a £23.4m budget gap, on top of raising council tax by 2.99% and a 2% Adult Social Care precept.
findings.detail: The Council faces £23.4m of net budget growth (from inflation, demand, and funding changes). To balance this without using general reserves, it is relying on £11.5m of directorate and service savings, additional council tax revenue of £2.2m from housing growth, and combined council tax rises of 4.99%.
findings.matters: Large savings programmes carry delivery risk, particularly when combined with near-maximum tax rises (4.99% is at the threshold where Government capping provisions can apply). Failure to deliver savings or a shortfall in council tax growth would create an in-year pressure.
findings.figures: £23.4m budget gap; £11.5m savings target; 2.99% council tax + 2% ASC precept (4.99% combined); £2.2m from tax base growth
findings.quote: In light of the gross budget requirement of £23.4m, the Council must identify budget savings and/or additional income of the same amount to ensure it is legally able to set a balanced budget. Directorate and service savings – the budget proposals include £11.5m of savings which either need to be delivered from 1 April 2026 or the services have adjusted the value of the savings to reflect the implementation date incorporated into the business cases which support each proposal.

findings.headline: High Needs Block (education) has a £6.5m deficit forecast for 2025/26, requiring £1.6m transfer from the mainstream schools block.
findings.detail: The High Needs Block, which funds education for children and young people with special educational needs from age 0–25, is forecasting an overall deficit of £6.5m in the current year. To address this, Schools Forum agreed to transfer £1.6m from the schools block to the high needs block in 2026/27.
findings.matters: This is a structural deficit in a ring-fenced funding stream, indicating rising SEN numbers and costs nationally that the council cannot fully control, and it is being addressed by reducing funding to mainstream schools.
findings.figures: £6.5m deficit in 2025/26; £1.6m transfer from schools block for 2026/27
findings.quote: Wakefield has reported within the 2025/26 financial year that the high needs block is forecasting to be in an overall deficit position of £6.5m. Therefore, the funding consultation has included proposals for redirection of funding from the school's block to the high needs block to help fund financial pressures. School Forum agreed to the proposal for redirection of £1.6m to the high needs block on 12th January 2026.

findings.headline: Adult social care placements are currently overspending, with higher caseloads and more complex (costlier) placements requiring £8.8m allocation plus £5.6m for market wage pressures.
findings.detail: The Council reports that in the current 2025/26 financial year, adults social care placement budgets are already overspent due to higher numbers of placements than budgeted and their increased complexity. The 2026/27 budget allocates £8.8m to address this overspend and support market sustainability, with a further £5.6m for National Living Wage impacts on commissioned care providers.
findings.matters: This is a real, current overspend in a high-risk service area, signalling that demographic and market pressures are outpacing budget assumptions and that future placements may cost more than anticipated.
findings.figures: £8.8m + £5.6m = £14.4m combined allocation for adult social care; overspend currently occurring in 2025/26
findings.quote: In the current financial year, adults social care packages of care placements budgets are overspent. This is due to higher number of placements than budgeted for, but also due to the complexity and resulting increasing cost of these placements. A combined £8.8m has been included for this. Furthermore, an additional £5.6m has been included in the budget proposals to provide funding for increases in the National Living Wage, which will impact the marketplace.

findings.headline: S151 Officer is newly appointed (September 2025) and must rely on external audit for assurance over prior years
findings.detail: The current S151 Officer was appointed only recently (September 2025) and explicitly states they rely on external audit as a key source of assurance. This is significant because the officer has limited time to build independent understanding of the council's financial position and disclaimed audit opinions create a gap.
findings.matters: A newly appointed finance officer who cannot rely on audited accounts to understand prior-year position creates governance risk; the council's finance leadership lacks deep knowledge of historical issues
findings.figures: Appointed September 2025
findings.quote: As the recently appointed S151 Officer (September 2025), I rely on external audit as a key source of assurance regarding the Council's financial position. While I can seek assurance over prior years' work and closing balances, I must highlight the gap in assurance that remains as a result of the disclaimed audit opinions since the 2022/23 accounts.

findings.headline: External auditors' financial sustainability recommendation has remained open since 2023/24
findings.detail: The external audit made a key recommendation on financial sustainability relating to ensuring the strategy to address reserve depletion is effective. This recommendation has been kept open for two years. The CFO acknowledges the auditors have now accepted the council has a strategy, but the long-standing finding indicates prior-year concerns.
findings.matters: A multi-year open audit finding on financial sustainability is a red flag for lenders; it shows auditors were concerned about reserve adequacy and the council's trajectory
findings.figures: Recommendation open since 2023/24 audit
findings.quote: In relation to the financial sustainability recommendation, which has been kept open since the 2023/24 audit, the auditors have acknowledged that the Council does indeed have a strategy to address the risks associated with reserve depletion.

findings.headline: Capital receipts from property disposals are assumed in the budget; timing and achievability are at risk
findings.detail: The budget assumes capital receipts from property and land disposals will support transformation projects and fund redundancy payments. The council acknowledges these receipts must be closely monitored and that properties carry large repair backlogs that can delay disposals, reduce values, or require unplanned investment.
findings.matters: Relying on property receipts for budget balance creates timing risk; large repair backlogs undermine the assumption that disposals will yield expected proceeds
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: Where the budget assumes the generation of capital receipts from property and land disposals to support transformation projects and fund redundancy payments, the timing of these receipts must be closely monitored and contingency actions identified should assumptions slip. The Council also carries a significant property related risk due to a large number of assets with substantial repair and maintenance backlogs, which can delay disposals, reduce achievable values, or require unplanned investment.

findings.headline: Strategic Regeneration Partnership viability depends on securing external funding from Homes England, WYCA and MHCLG
findings.detail: The council has entered a regeneration partnership to transform Wakefield City Centre but the project's financial viability depends on securing further funding from national and regional partners. There is explicit acknowledgement of financial risk if external funding is delayed or not secured at expected levels.
findings.matters: Large regeneration projects on external funding dependencies can easily overrun or be curtailed; any slippage cascades into budget pressures
findings.figures: Not quantified in this statement
findings.quote: The viability of the regeneration is financially dependent on securing further funds from national and regional partners such as Homes England, WYCA and MHCLG. There is therefore financial risk if this external funding is delayed or not secured at expected levels.

findings.headline: Audit opinions have been disclaimed since 2022/23 accounts, leaving a gap in assurance
findings.detail: The newly appointed S151 Officer (September 2025) explicitly highlights that disclaimed audit opinions since 2022/23 create a gap in assurance. While prior-year work and closing balances can be reviewed, this represents unresolved audit risk.
findings.matters: Disclaimed opinions on historical accounts suggest material audit findings; a lender cannot rely on audited financial statements and must assess the council blind on prior-year positions
findings.figures: Disclaimed opinions since 2022/23
findings.quote: As the recently appointed S151 Officer (September 2025), I rely on external audit as a key source of assurance regarding the Council's financial position. While I can seek assurance over prior years' work and closing balances, I must highlight the gap in assurance that remains as a result of the disclaimed audit opinions since the 2022/23 accounts.

findings.headline: Vacancy factor savings require active ongoing management to be delivered in 2026/27
findings.detail: A 2025 workforce reconciliation exercise revealed that historic HR data needed cleaning. The council acknowledges that vacancy factor savings will need active and ongoing management throughout 2026/27 to ensure delivery, and a more detailed assessment of vacancy factors will be needed in future budget-setting.
findings.matters: Vacancy factor savings depend on staff turnover and recruitment patterns; active management is required because the council does not actually control recruitment pipelines
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: This exercise confirmed that vacancy factor savings will need active and ongoing management throughout 2026/27 to ensure they are delivered. As part of future budget-setting processes, a more detailed assessment of vacancy factor levels across the Council will be required to ensure their continued appropriateness.

findings.headline: Placement costs in children's and adults' social care remain the most significant financial pressure
findings.detail: The CFO flags that placement costs in both children's and adults' social care are the most significant financial pressures experienced in 2025/26 and have been recognised in the 2026/27 budget. These are inherently volatile and demand-driven.
findings.matters: Uncontrollable demand pressures in social care are a chronic risk to councils; stating these are 'most significant' indicates they have already materially impacted the budget
findings.figures: Not quantified separately in this statement
findings.quote: Significant financial pressures experienced in 2025/26 have, where appropriate, been recognised in preparing the 2026/27 budget, or are subject to further actions to enable them to be managed- the most significant of which have been placement costs in both Childrens and Adults.

findings.headline: Identified directorate risks total £18.4m, against which reserves must act as buffer
findings.detail: Directorates have assessed their key budget areas and identified a maximum risk of £18.4m. The council states it would have sufficient reserves to address this, but this is measured against already-depleted reserves.
findings.matters: The magnitude of identified risk relative to reserves shows how tightly the council is balanced; any reserve depletion narrows the safety margin
findings.figures: £18.4m risk identified
findings.quote: As part of the budget process, directorates have undertaken a risk and opportunities assessment of their key budget areas and this has identified a maximum 'risk' of £18.4m. The Council would have sufficient financial reserves to address this should these risks materialise having factored in the £2m contribution to reserves planned as part of this budget report.

findings.headline: Reserves have been significantly depleted and cannot sustain further draws
findings.detail: The CFO states reserves have been significantly depleted in recent years and warns explicitly that any further depletion beyond what is in the budget would leave the council vulnerable. The council is now planning to *replenish* rather than draw from general reserves, a shift from prior strategy.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves reduce financial flexibility to absorb shocks; the explicit warning signals the council is near a threshold of concern
findings.figures: Reserve replenishment of £2m planned for 2026/27
findings.quote: Reserves have been significantly depleted in recent years and whilst they remain adequate for the 2026/27 financial year; the Chief Finance Officer would highlight that any further depletion beyond what is set out in the report is not recommended and would leave the Council vulnerable to financial issues in the future.

findings.headline: Savings delivery performance is declining: 88% in 2024/25, anticipated 66% in 2025/26, while planning £11.5m savings for 2026/27
findings.detail: The council achieved most of its savings over the past two years but the trend is deteriorating. The CFO explicitly flags that the declining delivery rate means savings for next year will need 'strong, proactive management and sustained focus', with a £2m contingency budget providing mitigation if savings slip.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether stated savings are actually being delivered; declining performance suggests execution risk on the £11.5m plan
findings.figures: 88% delivery in 2024/25, anticipated 66% in 2025/26, £11.5m planned for 2026/27, £2m contingency
findings.quote: The Council has achieved most of its approved savings over the past two years, delivering 88% in 2024/25 and an anticipated 66% in 2025/26. This performance provides some confidence that the £11.5m savings planned for 2026/27 are likely to be delivered. However, the declining delivery trend highlights the need for strong, proactive management and sustained focus to ensure future savings are achieved

findings.headline: Comprehensive asset condition surveys underway; council to report maintenance liabilities and long-term plan in Q2 2026/27
findings.detail: The council has commissioned 'Asset Verification and Condition reports' across its £504.5m operational property portfolio during 2025 and will develop a 'long-term maintenance plan'. Cabinet will be updated on findings in Q2 2026/27. This process suggests significant maintenance liabilities currently unquantified.
findings.matters: Councils often defer maintenance; condition surveys frequently reveal unfunded liabilities that require significant capital injection or additional borrowing, impacting financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Operational land and buildings net book value: £504.54m as at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: During 2025 the council has commissioned a series of Asset Verification and Condition reports which will inform a long-term maintenance plan. The aim is to update Cabinet in quarter two of 2026/27 on the outcomes of the surveys.

findings.headline: £115.9 million prudential borrowing programme with £28.7m in 2026/27 creates material ongoing revenue costs
findings.detail: The capital programme relies substantially on prudential borrowing (£115.9m over five years, 28% of total funding), with 2026/27 requiring £28.7m in new borrowing. The strategy acknowledges this creates 'revenue costs through interest charges and the minimum revenue provision' but quantification is in the November 2025 MTFS, not this document.
findings.matters: Large borrowing programmes materially impact revenue budgets through interest and MRP charges. Lenders must verify these costs remain sustainable and affordable within forecasted revenue.
findings.figures: Total prudential borrowing: £115,920k. 2026/27 borrowing: £28,718k (of £130,333k total 2026/27 capital expenditure)
findings.quote: Prudential borrowing increases the Council's capital financing requirement and creates revenue costs through interest charges and the minimum revenue provision (MRP).

findings.headline: Council will use capital receipts from asset sales to fund ongoing revenue costs in 2026/27
findings.detail: The strategy commits to using proceeds from asset disposals to fund 'qualifying revenue expenditure' in addition to capital assets in 2026/27, under statutory 'flexible use of capital receipts' powers. This uses one-time capital receipts to fund recurring costs, with the council noting this decision will be reviewed annually.
findings.matters: Using one-off capital receipts to cover revenue expenditure signals either a structural revenue funding gap or temporary pressure. Relying on asset disposals is unsustainable for ongoing costs.
findings.figures: Planned capital receipts 2026/27: £19.736m (to be split between revenue and capital). Total five-year capital receipts: £56.218m
findings.quote: In 2026/27, the Council will use capital receipts to fund qualifying revenue expenditure and will also fund new capital investment with short useful economic lives

findings.headline: Council replaces transparent MRP debt ceiling with discretionary capital contingency approach
findings.detail: The strategy abandons the previous rule capping Minimum Revenue Provision at 6.5% of adjusted net revenue budget, replacing it with a discretionary 'capital contingency allocation' that Cabinet can deploy to projects provided they stay within unspecified 'affordability parameters'. This removes a hard, published constraint.
findings.matters: Lenders rely on transparent, predictable debt constraints to assess credit risk. Replacing a fixed, published cap with discretionary contingency and undefined affordability parameters reduces visibility and makes debt sustainability harder to monitor.
findings.figures: Previously: MRP capped at 6.5% of adjusted net revenue budget. New approach: contingency allocation within 'affordability parameters identified at the time of finalising the budget'
findings.quote: This approach replaces the assumption that MRP does not exceed 6.5% of the Council's adjusted net revenue budget.

findings.headline: Council's corporate risk register identifies insufficient financial resources as a strategic threat to financial resilience
findings.detail: Strategic risk CORSTRR0057 explicitly warns: 'Due to increasing cost pressures and demands for services, coupled with limited and volatile funding, there is a risk that there is insufficient financial resources available to support the delivery of Council strategic and statutory duties, which could result in budget overspend in year and compromise the Council's longer-term financial resilience.'
findings.matters: The council's own risk assessment acknowledges potential budget overspend and questions about long-term financial resilience; this is the finance leadership's internal verdict on sustainability
findings.figures: Strategic risk CORSTRR0057; noted alongside organisational capacity risk CORSTRR0109
findings.quote: Due to increasing cost pressures and demands for services, coupled with limited and volatile funding, there is a risk that there is insufficient financial resources available to support the delivery of Council strategic and statutory duties, which could result in budget overspend in year and compromise the Council's longer-term financial resilience.

findings.headline: Capital financing costs consume 8.9% of the net revenue budget in a single year
findings.detail: The capital programme relies on £70.9m of prudential borrowing. In 2025/26 alone, net borrowing costs are forecast at £14.5m and Minimum Revenue Provision at £12.4m, totalling £26.9m in capital financing charges against a net revenue budget of £302.4m.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the fixed debt service burden; capital financing at 8.9% of budget constrains flexibility to respond to pressures and leaves limited headroom
findings.figures: £26.9m capital financing costs in 2025/26; £14.5m borrowing costs; £12.4m MRP; equivalent to 8.9% of net budget
findings.quote: The net borrowing costs, from P8 forecast that would amount to: £14.5m and overall capital financing costs for programme in 2025/26 would be £26.9m equivalent to 8.9% of the current net budget.

findings.headline: Council is funding revenue expenditure through prudential borrowing because other sources are exhausted
findings.detail: The council has reclassified revenue spend as capital for several years and now seeks approval for £2.6m in prudential borrowing to cover costs with no formal budget. Critically, the council describes this borrowing as 'as a last resort after options have been considered' and is 'currently reviewing the sustainability of this approach within its Medium Term Financial Strategy.'
findings.matters: Using capital borrowing to cover underlying revenue spend signals budget pressure and raises questions about debt sustainability and whether this pattern can continue
findings.figures: £2.6m prudential borrowing injection requested; baseline revenue budget £302.4m
findings.quote: The £2.6m will be funded through prudential borrowing as a last resort after options have been considered to fund short life assets through capital receipts in line with the council's current approach. The council is currently reviewing the sustainability of this approach within its Medium Term Financial Strategy and Capital Programme.

findings.paper_title: 2, - Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report for City of Wakefield Council
findings.headline: Unfunded pension liability of £39.4m is separately recognized on the balance sheet because the council cannot net it against the funded pension asset surplus.
findings.detail: Although the council's share of the West Yorkshire Pension Fund shows a surplus of £426m, IFRIC14 accounting principles cap the recognized asset at £nil. Separately, the council has an unfunded defined benefit obligation of £39.4m that cannot be offset against the funded surplus because there is no legal right to use the surplus to settle the unfunded obligation. This liability is reported separately on the balance sheet.
findings.matters: The £39.4m unfunded liability represents a real obligation that must be funded from reserves or future income. The separation of funded and unfunded elements shows the council's true exposure to pension obligations.
findings.figures: Funded asset surplus: £426m (capped at £nil by IFRIC14); Unfunded defined benefit obligation: £39.4m
findings.quote: Under IAS19, a funded asset position can only be netted off against an unfunded liability when, (a) the entity has a legally enforceable right to use a surplus in one plan to settle obligations under the other plan and (b) the entity intends to settle the obligations on a net basis or to release the surplus in one plan and settle its obligations under the other plan simultaneously. Our work indicated that none of these apply to the Council. Therefore, the Council has correctly reported this separately on the balance sheet as a long-term liability.

findings.paper_title: 2, - Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report for City of Wakefield Council
findings.headline: £19.5m of waste PFI plant and equipment assets cannot be verified to be materially correct due to lack of identifiable asset records since 2015.
findings.detail: The council capitalized £46.2m of plant, vehicles and equipment in 2015 when the waste PFI contract began, but has not maintained a breakdown of individual assets. Over 10 years, the council has depreciated, impaired and disposed of these assets without being able to identify which specific assets were affected. The current net book value is £19.5m. The auditors explicitly state they are 'unable to conclude the closing valuation as at 31 March 2025 of the Waste PFI plant vehicles and equipment are materially correct'.
findings.matters: An inability to verify nearly £20m in fixed assets indicates poor asset management controls and uncertainty over the true financial position. This raises questions about whether other capital assets are properly accounted for.
findings.figures: £46.2m capitalized in 2015; £19.5m net book value as at 31 March 2025; material to the audit
findings.quote: As a result, due to opening valuation uncertainty from 2015-16, with lack of identifiable assets with corresponding valuations, we are unable to conclude the closing valuation as at 31 March 2025 of the Waste PFI plant vehicles and equipment are materially correct. This will be reported within our audit opinion

findings.paper_title: 2, - Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report for City of Wakefield Council
findings.headline: Taxi driver restitution provision of £1.5m was missing from year-end provisions, reducing useable reserves.
findings.detail: The council had not included a £1.5m provision for taxi driver restitution dating back to a 2020 court decision. This was identified during audit and the council has agreed to adjust the accounts. The adjustment directly reduces the council's general fund (useable reserves) by £1.5m.
findings.matters: The omission of a known legal obligation from provisions means the council overstated its available reserves and underestimated its liabilities. This is a control failure affecting the reliability of the financial position.
findings.figures: £1.5m provision adjustment; reduces useable reserves by £1.5m
findings.quote: All the adjustments identified have no impact on the Authority's useable reserves, except for a £1.5m adjustment relating to restitution for taxi drivers within the district which was not included in the provisions for the year ended 31 March 2025. This would reduce Authority's useable reserves by £1.5m.

findings.paper_title: 2, - Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report for City of Wakefield Council
findings.headline: Ongoing significant weakness in financial sustainability arrangements, with only one key recommendation carried forward from prior year.
findings.detail: The audit identifies financial sustainability as an area of significant weakness that persists from the prior year. In 2024, three key recommendations were raised; two have been addressed but one remains unresolved. The auditor has made a new key recommendation and two improvement recommendations for this area.
findings.matters: An ongoing significant weakness in financial sustainability is precisely what lenders assess when evaluating whether a council can sustain its obligations and manage financial pressures.
findings.figures: Three prior-year key recommendations, two addressed, one ongoing
findings.quote: Financial sustainability: an ongoing significant weakness in arrangements for financial sustainability identified and a key recommendation made. We also raised two improvement recommendations.

findings.paper_title: 2, - Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report for City of Wakefield Council
findings.headline: Auditors cannot give a clean opinion due to inability to verify opening balances after two years of disclaimed opinions.
findings.detail: The council received disclaimed audit opinions for both 2023 and 2024. This means auditors have no assurance over opening balances for 2025. Although they have tested 2025 transactions, the lack of opening balance assurance means the audit opinion will be modified. The auditors state they 'have been unable to undertake sufficient work to support an unmodified audit opinion in advance of the backstop date of 27 February 2026'.
findings.matters: A modified audit opinion signals material uncertainty about the financial statements and would concern any lender evaluating the council's creditworthiness.
findings.figures: £426m pension asset capped at £nil; £39.4m unfunded pension liability; total council expenditure materiality set at £13m
findings.quote: Due to the challenges of undertaking an audit where the previous two years' audits (2022-23 and 2023-24) were subject to backstop-related disclaimed audit opinions, we have been unable to undertake sufficient work to support an unmodified audit opinion in advance of the backstop date of 27 February 2026

findings.headline: Contracts register still not complete or accurate after prior year recommendation; internal audit gave limited assurance on gifts and hospitality compliance
findings.detail: Internal audit found the Council's contracts register remains incomplete and inaccurate, a finding that has persisted from 2022-23. The auditor states this 'continue[s] to hold' and notes 'we see improvement in this area as a priority for the Council as failure to do so could result in either sudden or gradual loss of value from failure to recognise and manage contract risk appropriately.' Separately, internal audit issued limited assurance on gifts and hospitality policy, finding no central file of high-value gifts or gifts offered to the Chief Executive or Corporate Directors.
findings.matters: Incomplete contract records mean the council cannot verify all procurement and contractual activity complies with its own rules or legal requirements; combined with limited assurance on gifts/hospitality compliance, this increases governance risk and reputational exposure.
findings.figures: Contracts register still not fully complete and accurate; internal audit limited assurance on gifts/hospitality audit; high priority recommendation on central file of gifts
findings.quote: Internal audit's findings in 2022-23 of inconsistent contract management arrangements across the Council and a lack of a complete contracts register continue to hold. The Council appointed a new Commercial Director to post from September 2024... However, progress in validating existing contract information and ensuring that all operational information on contracts is not held in a central area remains outstanding.

findings.headline: Capital programme saw 29% slippage (£27.6m on £95.2m budget) continuing a pattern from prior year; largest slippage in regeneration
findings.detail: The 2024-25 capital programme saw £27.6m (29%) slippage against a revised budget of £95.2m. This continues a pattern from 2023-24 where slippage was £16.5m. The largest variance was in Regeneration, Environment and Economic Growth (£13.6m), nearly half the total. Although the programme was revised down during the year from £126.7m to £95.2m, the scale of slippage remains significant and carry-forward into 2025-26 has increased the profiled budget to £183.3m, 'heightening delivery risk.'
findings.matters: Repeated capital slippage suggests either planning discipline issues or unforeseen constraints; a £183.3m profiled 2025-26 capital budget with a track record of missing targets creates risk to strategic priorities and may indicate value-for-money issues in project management.
findings.figures: £27.6m slippage (29%) on £95.2m revised budget in 2024-25; £13.6m (nearly 50%) in Regeneration directorate; carry-forward into 2025-26 creates £183.3m profiled budget
findings.quote: In 2024-25, the Council's actual expenditure was £67.8m against a revised budget of £95.2m (the original capital budget for 2024-25 was £126.7m), resulting in slippage of £27.6m (29%). This follows a similar pattern to 2023-24, where slippage was £16.5m.

findings.headline: £29m savings programme for 2025-26 only 65% on track, with £10.2m delayed or at risk; would require cutting 249.1 FTE posts
findings.detail: To balance the 2025-26 budget, the Council must deliver £29m of savings from a total £39.4m challenge. However, only £18.8m (65%) is on track, leaving £10.2m 'either delayed or at risk, creating further risk and budgetary pressures.' Full implementation would require reduction of 249.1 FTE posts. In 2024-25, 7 of the £21.4m savings target were not delivered entirely (£2m) and 6 others fell short (£1m shortfall).
findings.matters: The council's financial recovery depends on delivery of savings that are already showing slippage; missed targets would force further reserve draws and potentially require harder decisions on service delivery.
findings.figures: £29m savings target for 2025-26; £18.8m (65%) on track; £10.2m delayed or at risk; would require 249.1 FTE reduction; 2024-25 saw £2m of target not delivered and £1m shortfall on others
findings.quote: The level of challenge in delivering savings is increasing, with the Council noting that implementation of the full budget savings proposals would mean a reduction of 249.1 FTE full-time equivalent posts. However, while £18.8m (65%) of the £29m savings target is on track, £10.2m is either delayed or at risk, creating further risk and budgetary pressures.

findings.headline: 2024-25 overspend of £4.8m funded from reserves despite new control policies, with 2025-26 forecasting £7.1m further overspend
findings.detail: The Council ended 2024-25 with an overspend of £4.8m (1.7% of original £285m budget), funded from reserves. Main drivers were children's and young people's services (£6m) and rising demand and costs for external residential provision. Early 2025-26 reporting shows a £7.1m forecast overspend (2.3% of revenue budget), with Adult Social Care £3.1m and Children's Services £3.0m. The auditor notes: 'An overspend on this scale could lead to net use of reserves, which would not be in line with the Council's strategy.'
findings.matters: The council's stated commitment to stop drawing reserves for budget-setting is being immediately tested by uncontrolled service overspends, particularly in social care demand—the hardest cost to control.
findings.figures: 2024-25 overspend £4.8m (1.7% of £285m budget); 2025-26 forecast £7.1m (2.3% of net revenue budget); Adult Social Care £3.1m, Children's Services £3.0m
findings.quote: The Council ended 2024-25 with an overspend of £4.8m (1.7% of the original £285m budget). The overspend was funded from the Council's financial resilience reserve and primarily driven by overspends in children's and young people's services (£6m) and rising demand and increased costs for external residential provision.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant turned into deficit for the first time, with in-year overspend of £4.6m on independent placements
findings.detail: Wakefield reported its first cumulative DSG deficit of £0.8m at year-end 2024-25. The in-year overspend was £4.6m, driven by increased EHCP numbers and independent placements. The auditor specifically flags that deficits in this area 'can escalate quickly and take time to control effectively' and notes the move into deficit is 'concerning given the Council's overall low reserve levels.'
findings.matters: A new deficit area with demand-driven cost pressures is harder to control than one-off issues; combined with low reserves, this could trigger rapid deterioration and put pressure on the general fund after the statutory override expires in March 2028.
findings.figures: Cumulative DSG deficit £0.8m; in-year overspend £4.6m, primarily in High Needs Block
findings.quote: The Council reported a £0.8m cumulative DSG deficit at 31 March 2025. While this is still a small deficit, the in-year overspend was more significant at £4.6m.

findings.headline: Reserves depleted by 27% in one year, now at £81.9m with structural budget gaps to 2030
findings.detail: Total reserves fell from £112.8m (March 2024) to £81.9m (March 2025), a £30.9m reduction. Earmarked reserves fell from £96.5m to £65.6m. The Council faces budget gaps of £35.8m in 2025-26, £15.0m in 2026-27, £10.9m in 2027-28, £12.7m in 2028-29, and £13.5m in 2029-30. While new leadership has stopped using financial resilience reserves for budget-setting from 2025-26, the downward trajectory of reserves in 2024-25 reflects historic decisions.
findings.matters: A lender assessing debt capacity needs to know whether the council can absorb financial shocks; this trajectory suggests limited headroom even with the council's stated commitment to rebuild reserves.
findings.quote: Total reserves fell from £112.8m at 31 March 2024 to £81.9m at 31 March 2025, a reduction of £30.9m (27%).

findings.paper_title: 4 - Treasury Management Mid-Year Report for the Period Ending 30 September 2025
findings.headline: Council identifies strategic risk of insufficient financial resources on corporate risk register
findings.detail: Corporate risk register (CORSTRR0057) flags risk that "increasing cost pressures and demands for services, coupled with limited and volatile funding" could result in budget overspend and compromise "longer-term financial resilience." No current-year budget overspend is reported, but risk is explicitly managed at strategic level.
findings.matters: Council's own assessment that medium-term financial sustainability is at risk due to cost/funding mismatch; combines with reserve depletion and capital cuts to suggest gathering budget pressure.
findings.figures: No specific figures provided; risk flagged as strategic issue but no quantified budget gap disclosed
findings.quote: Due to increasing cost pressures and demands for services, coupled with limited and volatile funding, there is a risk that there is insufficient financial resources available to support the delivery of Council strategic and statutory duties, which could result in budget overspend in year and compromise the Council's longer-term financial resilience.

findings.paper_title: 4 - Treasury Management Mid-Year Report for the Period Ending 30 September 2025
findings.headline: Internal reserves forecast to deplete, forcing greater reliance on external borrowing
findings.detail: Council states that while it has previously maintained strategy of using internal cash balances as alternative to external borrowing, "internal balances are forecast to reduce as reserves are released creating the need to borrow externally." This marks shift from internal to external financing and reduces financial flexibility.
findings.matters: Drawdown of internal reserves limits council's buffer against financial shocks and indicates underlying funding gap that must be financed externally.
findings.figures: No specific reserve balances or depletion rates quantified in this report
findings.quote: Although internal balances are forecast to reduce as reserves are released creating the need to borrow externally.

findings.paper_title: 4 - Treasury Management Mid-Year Report for the Period Ending 30 September 2025
findings.headline: Borrowing strategy shifted from long-term to short-term due to PWLB rate rises, creating refinancing risk
findings.detail: Council abandoned asset-backed long-term borrowing strategy that had been "financially advantageous" in response to higher Public Works Loan Board rates. Now adopting shorter-term borrowing at 4.2%-4.6% and plans medium-term borrowing in 2025/26 to spread debt maturities. Strategy will revert to long-term "when rates stabilise at some point in the medium term."
findings.matters: Short-term dependence creates material refinancing risk if rates remain elevated or rise further; strategy change indicates cost pressure driving financial decisions.
findings.figures: Short-term borrowing rates 4.2%-4.6%, 10-year PWLB gilt yield 4.70% at end September, Bank of England rates cut from 4.50% to 4.00% over period
findings.quote: This strategy has been reviewed considering the impact of the rise in Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) rates and a shorter-term borrowing strategy has been adopted until rates stabilise at some point in the medium term. An element of medium-term borrowing will be undertaken in 2025/26 to enable the Council to spread its debt maturity profile and reduce the risk of relying on the availability of significant levels of short-term debt.

findings.paper_title: 4 - Treasury Management Mid-Year Report for the Period Ending 30 September 2025
findings.headline: Capital programme reduced by £43m (31%) mid-year with only 27% spent in first six months
findings.detail: Council revised capital expenditure from £135.3m budget to £92.6m approved at Q2, a variance of £42.7m. Largest reductions are Regeneration/Environment (£26.1m), Transformation (£8.9m), and Schools (£8.5m). Actual spend to end September stands at £25.2m, meaning significant acceleration would be needed in H2 to meet revised profile, or further slippage is likely.
findings.matters: A 31% mid-year cut to capital programme signals either delivery challenges, reprioritisation under budget pressure, or funding constraints; slow H2 progress creates refinancing and cashflow risk.
findings.figures: Budget £135.3m, revised £92.6m, variance (£42.7m), actual spend Q2 £25.2m (27% of revised profile)
findings.quote: The table below shows the revised estimates for capital expenditure and the changes since the capital programme was approved at the Budget Council in March 2025.

findings.headline: Capital programme governance arrangements are under formal review, suggesting current controls may be inadequate.
findings.detail: The council has initiated a review of capital governance to embed the Duty of Best Value. The outcome will be reported to Cabinet, implying that current governance structures are not seen as sufficient. Audit Committee reporting on major capital schemes is also being reconsidered as part of this review.
findings.matters: Ongoing governance review indicates potential weaknesses in project oversight, approval, or risk management that could allow problems to go undetected until spending occurs.
findings.figures: Six-monthly risk reporting to Audit Committee; governance review ongoing
findings.quote: Governance arrangements for the Capital Programme are currently under review with a view to further embedding the Duty of Best Value. Updated governance arrangements will be reported to Cabinet when finalised.

findings.headline: External funding expectations have shifted: £0.85m originally planned for CIL is now split between CIL and prudential borrowing, suggesting external funding volatility.
findings.detail: Ward projects totalling £0.85m were originally expected to be funded from Community Infrastructure Levy. Project scoping has now clarified that only part of this is CIL-eligible, requiring the council to fund the remainder through borrowing instead. This mid-year funding repricing indicates CIL availability or eligibility is less certain than initially planned.
findings.matters: Funding sources shifting mid-year from external to borrowed funds increases borrowing pressure and suggests forward planning around grants or external revenue may be unreliable.
findings.figures: £0.85m ward projects; mix of CIL and prudential borrowing; additional £0.5m highways from CIL identification
findings.quote: ward projects that were originally intended to be funded from CIL totalling £0.85m as reported to September Cabinet, to be funded from a mix of CIL and prudential borrowing as detailed project scoping has clarified eligibility to CIL funding.

findings.headline: MRP charge of £12.4m (4.1% of revenue budget) is rising and approaches the agreed tolerance ceiling of 6.5%.
findings.detail: MRP for 2025/26 is £12.4m against a net revenue budget of £302.4m. While currently within agreed tolerances, the trajectory is upward as more capital schemes funded through borrowing complete and enter the MRP charge. As borrowing increases, MRP will consume a larger proportion of revenue resources.
findings.matters: Rising MRP commitments progressively restrict the council's revenue flexibility and ability to invest in services or absorb unexpected cost pressures.
findings.figures: £12.4m MRP; £302.4m net revenue budget; 4.1% of budget; 6.5% tolerance agreed
findings.quote: The MRP charge for 2025/26 (which is based on expenditure up to 31st March 2025) is expected to be £12.4m measured against a net revenue budget of £302.4m. This is within the capital strategy tolerances agreed at budget council equivalent to 4.1% of the net revenue budget.

findings.headline: Only 41% of planned capital spend is contractually committed or spent at Q2, creating significant risk of delivery slippage and unfulfilled annual budget.
findings.detail: Actual expenditure and commitments at the end of quarter 2 stand at £38.367m against profiled spend of £92.579m (41%). The council explicitly flags that low contractual commitment halfway through the year poses a risk of end-of-year slippage, suggesting either unrealistic budgeting or delivery capacity constraints.
findings.matters: Persistent slippage indicates either budgets are not deliverable or there are underlying project management or capacity issues; both concern a potential lender about forward forecasting reliability.
findings.figures: £38.367m actual/committed; £92.579m profiled (41% progress)
findings.quote: there continues to be a risk of slippage at year end given the low level of contractually committed projects halfway through the financial year.

findings.headline: £118.9m of prudential borrowing funds 40% of the five-year capital programme, creating ongoing revenue commitments through MRP and borrowing costs.
findings.detail: The capital programme is underpinned by £118.945m of prudential borrowing against a total revised programme of £297.806m. This creates direct revenue implications: the council calculates that every £10m of prudentially borrowed capital spend requires approximately £0.7m in annual revenue funding at a 5% interest rate over 25 years.
findings.matters: High levels of prudential borrowing reduce the council's revenue flexibility and constrain its ability to respond to service pressures or unexpected costs.
findings.figures: £118.945m prudential borrowing; £297.806m total programme; £0.7m annual revenue cost per £10m borrowed
findings.quote: the revised capital programme is underpinned by £118.945m of prudential borrowing and the delivery profile directly impacts on the Council's revenue budget strategy. All projects that are funded through prudential borrowing have revenue implications through Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) and borrowing costs.

findings.headline: £50m of short-term inter-authority borrowing requires refinancing during 2025/26
findings.detail: Total gross borrowing stands at £339m, of which £50m (15%) is inter-authority lending. The paper states this short-term borrowing is "due to the overall financial position and the underlying need to borrow for capital purposes" and must be refinanced during the remainder of the financial year.
findings.matters: The need to refinance significant short-term inter-authority borrowing signals cash flow or funding pressure, which could indicate financial stress or constrained access to longer-term funding
findings.figures: £50m inter-authority lending; £339m total gross borrowing; 15% of total
findings.quote: The high level of the inter-authority borrowing is short-term and due to the overall financial position and the underlying need to borrow for capital purposes (the Capital Financing Requirement - CFR), refinancing of inter-authority borrowing will need to be undertaken during the remainder of the financial year.

findings.headline: Q1 2025/26 capital spend at only 6.45% of annual profile suggests continued delivery risk
findings.detail: Actual capital expenditure in Q1 2025/26 was £7.812m against a profiled spend of £121.076m (6.45%). Combined with the prior year's 29% slippage, this low early-year burn rate indicates the council may struggle to deliver its full annual programme.
findings.matters: Persistent underspend against profile demonstrates delivery challenges that affect both borrowing utilisation and the council's ability to achieve its strategic capital objectives
findings.figures: £7.812m actual; £121.076m profiled; 6.45% of planned spend
findings.quote: Actual expenditure at the end of quarter 1 was £7.812m (6.45% of profiled spend of £121.076m)

findings.headline: Significant capital slippage in prior year: 29% underspend against revised programme
findings.detail: Actual capital expenditure in 2024/25 was £67.768m against a revised programme of £95.231m, resulting in £27.463m of slippage. Officers acknowledge this would create an "unrealistic and undeliverable profile" if simply carried forward, and Q2 work will include "constructive challenge to directorates" to reprofile schemes.
findings.matters: Significant prior-year slippage raises questions about the council's ability to deliver its capital programme, affecting both strategic objectives and revenue budget assumptions
findings.figures: £67.768m actual; £95.231m revised programme; £27.463m slippage (29%)
findings.quote: the actual expenditure in 2024/25 was a total of £67.768m, resulting in £27.463m of slippage against a revised programme of £95.231m

findings.headline: Capital programme relies on £119.777m of prudential borrowing over five years
findings.detail: The council's revised capital programme of £273.172m is underpinned by £119.777m of prudential borrowing. The MRP charge for 2025/26 is forecast at £12.353m (4.1% of the net revenue budget), well within the 6.5% affordability tolerance, but the scale of borrowing directly impacts revenue budget strategy.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand the council's total debt commitment and ability to service it through the revenue budget
findings.figures: £119.777m prudential borrowing; £273.172m total capital programme; £12.353m MRP charge; 4.1% of net revenue budget
findings.quote: the revised capital programme is underpinned by £119.777m of prudential borrowing and the delivery profile directly impacts on the Council's revenue budget strategy.

news_drafts.headline: The historical MRP overpayment that has been subsidising revenue budgets will be fully consumed by end of 2026/27, creating a permanent revenue cost increase from 2027/28.
news_drafts.lead: This represents a quantified and material increase in future revenue costs (approximately £7m+ annually based on current MRP levels) that will reduce financial flexibility unless revenue rises or other costs reduce to offset it.

news_drafts.headline: Capital programme underspent significantly for the second consecutive year, with £54.9m less spent than budgeted.
news_drafts.lead: A lender needs to assess whether the council can deliver its investment plans. Two consecutive years of major slippage suggests potential execution or planning challenges that could affect service delivery and future financing needs.

news_drafts.headline: Future-year transformation savings (2026/27–2029/30) are not yet quantified despite £5m+ in committed costs
news_drafts.lead: Committing capital expenditure without identified or quantified benefits creates execution risk; failure to deliver the expected transformation savings would force unexpected revenue reductions
